ourStory.heading: Our Story
ourStory.howWeMetDescription: How John and Diana's story began — from an unexpected first date to shared adventures, family, and saying "I do" in Quito.
ourStory.howWeMetP1: Our story began in the most unexpected way. What was supposed to be an ordinary day turned into our first date and the beginning of something truly special. We started with simple errands at Home Depot—not exactly the classic romantic setting—but somewhere between conversations and spending time together, the day slowly became something much more memorable.
ourStory.howWeMetP2: From there, we went to enjoy sushi, explored the mall, and ended the day with sweet macarons. It wasn't extravagant—it was genuine, easy, and full of moments that made us realize how much we enjoyed being together.
ourStory.howWeMetP3: Not long after, we took our first trip together to Tampa, Florida, where we visited friends and created unforgettable memories. That trip became the first of many adventures. Over time, we shared birthdays, family visits, countless trips, laughter, and everyday moments that became the foundation of our relationship.
ourStory.howWeMetP4: Each experience brought us closer and reminded us how beautiful life is when shared with the right person. Through all the adventures, celebrations, and growing together, our love continued to become stronger.
ourStory.howWeMetP5: And now, here we are—getting married and preparing to celebrate this next chapter surrounded by the people we love most. We cannot wait to say "I do" and share this incredible moment with all of you.
ourStory.howWeMetClosing: Thank you for being part of our journey.
ourStory.heritageBody: Imanalla, welcome. Diana's roots are in Otavalo, an Andean community known for its Kichwa language, music, and extraordinary weaving traditions. Otavalo textiles carry generations of artistry, patience, and identity, while Andean values honor family, reciprocity, and Pachamama—Mother Earth. As John and Diana begin married life, they carry those roots with gratitude. This celebration also honors kuyay, the Kichwa word for love: love of family, love of place, and the love that brings all of us together in Quito.
ourStory.heroAlt: John and Diana sharing a kiss beneath a pearl-studded veil, with city buildings and blue sky behind them
ourStory.timelineIntro: Six years from a Home Depot run to "I do" in Quito.

altitude.heading: Plan for the altitude — safety comes first
altitude.compactCta: Read our altitude tips on the Travel page →
altitude.intro: Quito sits at 2,850 m / 9,350 ft. The thinner air affects almost everyone — even fit, experienced travelers feel it. The high-altitude sun and dry mountain air also dehydrate you faster than at sea level, so a few simple habits make a real difference in how good you feel for the wedding week.
items: Hydrate aggressively. Drink water steadily all day — much more than you would at home. Limit caffeine and alcohol for the first 24–48 hours; both speed up dehydration at altitude.
Take it easy your first day. Sleep in, walk slowly, and skip strenuous hikes, gym sessions, and heavy meals. Save the late nights for closer to the wedding.
Arrive 1–2 days early if you can. Acclimating before the ceremony makes the celebration far more enjoyable — and dramatically reduces the risk of feeling unwell on the big day.
Eat light, carbohydrate-forward meals at first. Soups, breads, fruit, and Ecuadorian almuerzos sit better than rich dinners those first nights.
Try coca tea (mate de coca). It's offered at most hotels and helps with mild headache or nausea. Ibuprofen or acetaminophen also eases altitude headaches.
Pack SPF 30+ sunscreen and a brimmed hat. UV is intense at 2,850 m even on cloudy days, and sunburn worsens dehydration.
altitude.extraCare: If you smoke, are 60 or older, or have heart, lung, or blood-pressure conditions, please talk to your doctor before traveling. Consider arriving an extra day or two early, pacing yourself even more slowly, and asking your provider about altitude medication (acetazolamide / Diamox) as a preventive option. Bring any regular medications in your carry-on.
altitude.help: A severe headache that doesn't respond to medication, persistent shortness of breath at rest, repeated vomiting, confusion, or chest pain are warning signs of altitude sickness and require immediate medical attention. Quito's emergency number is 911 (English-speaking dispatchers available), and any hotel front desk can summon a doctor or arrange transport.

travel.heading: Travel
travel.heroAlt: A panoramic view of Quito spread across the Andean basin, seen from the El Panecillo overlook
travel.airportInfoBody: Fly into Mariscal Sucre International Airport (UIO), about 45–60 minutes from Old Town depending on traffic. Official airport taxis are typically about $26 to central Quito, and the airport express bus is about $8.
travel.altitudeTip: Quito sits at about 9,350 feet / 2,850 meters. Plan a gentle first day, drink water, and give yourself time to acclimate.
travel.weatherTip: March is part of the wet season. Expect cool mornings and evenings, possible rain, strong high-altitude sun, and temperatures around 50–69°F. Pack layers and a light rain jacket.
travel.currencyTip: Ecuador uses the U.S. Dollar. Small bills are helpful for taxis, markets, and tips.
travel.safetyTip: Use official taxis or trusted ride-share options, keep valuables close in busy areas, and take normal big-city precautions in Old Town.
travel.stayIntro: A few 4★ and 5★ hotels in Quito's Old Town, within easy walking distance of the Basílica and Hotel Plaza Grande. Estimated rates are approximate; please verify for March 2027.
travel.sightseeingIntro: If you are extending your trip, here are some of the most memorable things to see in and around Quito.

sightseeing.name: Old Town walking tour
sightseeing.details: Plaza Grande, La Compañía (gold-leaf interior), San Francisco, and Calle La Ronda — all walkable from the Plaza.

sightseeing.name: TelefériQo cable car
sightseeing.details: Cable car climbs to about 3,945 m for sweeping city and Andes views; round-trip about $8.50. Go early before clouds.

sightseeing.name: Mitad del Mundo
sightseeing.details: Equator monument about 45 minutes north of Quito; entry around $5. Combine with Museo Solar Inti Ñan for fun gravity demonstrations.

sightseeing.name: Mindo Cloud Forest
sightseeing.details: Birding and waterfalls about 2 hours northwest. 450+ species recorded — a local guide makes the morning unforgettable.

sightseeing.name: Otavalo Market (Saturday)
sightseeing.details: Famous Andean textile market about 2 hours north — best experienced on a Saturday morning.

sightseeing.name: Galápagos · Cuenca · Amazon
sightseeing.details: Multi-day add-ons. Galápagos and Cuenca need domestic flights; the Amazon is reached via Coca. Build in extra time and check vaccine guidance for the jungle.

travel.healthBody: No special vaccines are required for Quito itself. Yellow fever vaccine is recommended if extending to the Amazon and required by some countries on re-entry. Drink bottled or filtered water (hotels usually provide it), pack SPF 30+ and a hat for the intense high-altitude sun, and give your body 24–48 hours to acclimate before strenuous activities. Pharmacies ("farmacias") are common throughout Quito for over-the-counter needs.
travel.connectivityIntro: Several easy options for data and calls while you're in Ecuador.

connectivity.name: US carrier roaming
connectivity.details: T-Mobile, Verizon, and AT&T plans typically include Ecuador data, though speeds may be slower than at home. Verify your plan before flying.

connectivity.name: eSIM (recommended)
connectivity.details: Airalo and Holafly sell Ecuador eSIMs from about $5–15 for 1–2 GB. Install before flying and activate on arrival — no SIM swap needed.

connectivity.name: Local SIM
connectivity.details: Claro and Movistar sell prepaid SIMs at UIO airport for around $10 with a few GB of data. Bring an unlocked phone.

connectivity.name: WiFi
connectivity.details: Most hotels, cafés, and restaurants in Quito offer free WiFi to customers.

privacy.heading: Privacy notice
privacy.intro: This page explains how John & Diana handle the information you share with our wedding website. It is a small personal site for invited guests — nothing here is sold, shared with advertisers, or passed to third parties.

sections.title: What we collect
sections.body: When you RSVP, we collect your name, your party members' names, your responses (attending or not attending), and any dietary restrictions, song requests, or notes you choose to share. If you provide an email address or phone number, we store those too so we can send updates and reminders.

sections.title: Why we collect it
sections.body: We use this information only for wedding logistics — meal counts for the kitchen, seating charts, song queue, transportation planning, and a small number of reminder messages before the RSVP deadline.

sections.title: About the reminder text messages
sections.body: If you provide a phone number, we may send up to a few reminder texts before the RSVP deadline of November 15, 2026. Messages come from a toll-free number registered to this wedding website. Reply STOP at any time to stop receiving messages, or HELP for support. Message and data rates from your carrier may apply. We do not share your phone number with anyone — not other guests, not vendors, not third parties.

sections.title: How long we keep your data
sections.body: We delete all RSVP responses, phone numbers, and email addresses within 60 days after the wedding (by mid-May 2027). Photos taken at the wedding itself are kept separately and aren't affected by this notice.

sections.title: Who sees your information
sections.body: Only John and Diana. We do not sell, rent, or share your information with anyone, including our wedding vendors. Meal counts and dietary restrictions are provided to our caterer as anonymized totals.

sections.title: Your choices
sections.body: You can ask us to delete your information at any time, update it, or send you a copy of what we have. Just email johnmlien@outlook.com and we'll handle it within a few days.

sections.title: Anonymous usage analytics
sections.body: We use Microsoft Application Insights (an Azure service) to see which pages get visited, whether anything errored out, and which features are used most. The data is anonymous — no names, no RSVP details, no contact info — just things like page views, click counts, and error reports. It helps us notice if a button is broken or a page isn't loading for someone. No third-party trackers are used and the data stays in our Azure subscription.

sections.title: Contact
sections.body: Questions or requests: johnmlien@outlook.com. The website is operated by John Lien personally for John & Diana's March 13, 2027 wedding.

heritage.title: A note on heritage
heritage.paragraph: Imanalla, welcome. Diana's roots are in Otavalo, an Andean community known for its Kichwa language, music, and extraordinary weaving traditions. Otavalo textiles carry generations of artistry, patience, and identity, while Andean values honor family, reciprocity, and Pachamama—Mother Earth. As John and Diana begin married life, they carry those roots with gratitude. This celebration also honors kuyay, the Kichwa word for love: love of family, love of place, and the love that brings all of us together in Quito.
